brief.head: A dish to start with
brief.text: India’s first important software centre by a global company, as Ajay Shah recalls it, was Texas Instruments’. It needed a satellite dish, and Montek Singh Ahluwalia helped win permission. {028-S04}

brief.head: Hired by hand wave
brief.text: In a Kathmandu corridor around 1974, Manmohan Singh told Vijay Kelkar, “So you will come to work with us, won’t you?” Kelkar felt obliged to say yes. {028-S21}

brief.head: Saamagri taiyaar hai
brief.text: Handing power to Atal Bihari Vajpayee in May 1996, Narasimha Rao told him the material for the nuclear test was ready. His government had left the decision to the next. {028-S11}

brief.head: ‘Why me?’
brief.text: Almost every accomplished woman Amit Varma invites on his podcast asks “Why me?”, he said. The men never do. He sees it as a leftover of a patriarchal past. {028-C10}

brief.head: Hello and goodbye
brief.text: In 2005 KP Krishnan burst into Ajay Shah’s finance ministry office to say he had just joined. It was Shah’s last day there, and the day his mother died. {028-S22}

thought.text: His greatest quality was his loneliness.

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah pitch a web series
lead.head: Freedom, the second time round
body: Amit Varma wants a web series made about India’s economic reforms, and he knows how that sounds. “People will say, what a crazy geeky subject,” he said. “And I’m like, yeah. But it’s incredibly important.”

The reforms, from 1991 onwards, got hundreds of millions of people out of poverty. They were also, Varma said, the work of “a bunch of people who were fighting behind the scenes in what I think is a great freedom movement”. {028-C01}
Like the original freedom fighters, he said, they worked for principles that brought them no immediate reward. He calls the series *The Reformers*.
Ajay Shah, who had asked for one of the greatest stories never told, added scenes of his own, and found himself written into one.
## A cast of five
The pilot opens in the early 1960s in the rooms of Balbir Singh, an economics professor at St Stephen’s College, Delhi. A shy young Montek Singh Ahluwalia sits at the back.
Varma built the series on five or six human stories, the ones he knew best: Ahluwalia, PV Narasimha Rao, the economists Isher Judge Ahluwalia and Padma Desai, and KP Krishnan of the finance ministry.
Montek Singh Ahluwalia’s thread is patience. He came home in the late 1970s to a finance ministry post with no glory, and worked in the background for years.

Varma cited the Abraham Lincoln line about spending five of six hours sharpening the axe. When the 1991 crisis came, the axe was sharp, and the M document, a roadmap for reform, was already written. {028-C02}
Rao, in Varma’s telling, was a true believer and a man of deep learning, not merely the politician who managed other men’s reforms.
Krishnan carries the 2008 crisis season, and the image that opens and closes the series: a man swimming laps, alone.
## Grace across elections
Shah’s stories turned on reform as a relay. With elections coming, P Chidambaram left inflation targeting to his successor rather than rush it through, and Arun Jaitley took it up.
“That’s the decency and grace by which we can build complex projects across elections,” Shah said. {028-C05}
It also needs people who stay. “Ministers come, ministers go,” Shah said; a professional elite must carry the memory. That capability, he warned, is not working as it used to.
## Why they kept going

Varma asked how anyone keeps a sense of purpose while defending ideas such as positive-sum games and spontaneous order, so easily caricatured as anti-poor. Yet these people, he said, gave decades to the long game, not columns from an armchair. {028-C07}

Shah’s first answer was wounded pride. India’s elite had believed it was the post-colonial country certain to succeed, the land of Tagore, Ramanujan, Nehru and Gandhi. The years from the 1962 China war to the Emergency, as East Asia grew rich, felt like a personal affront.
“You may have been a Marxist when you were young, but it ain’t working and you have to change course,” he said. {028-C03}

His second answer was ideas. A simple political-economy story, of the Mancur Olson kind, says firms behind 300 per cent tariffs would never let them fall. Yet duties fell year after year until 2007–08, because the reformers read and argued.
Shah ended by recommending Varma’s podcast, *The Seen and the Unseen*, as oral history, then signed off as if he hosted it. Varma kept the fumble in.

second.label: Import licences
second.head: Stuck with the old model
second.deck: In 1983 an import licence locked Infosys into older, dearer computers
body: In 1983 Narayana Murthy of Infosys wanted to import Data General computers, state of the art, with three removable hard drives of 200 MB each. “Can you imagine 200 whole MB?” Amit Varma asked. For months, Murthy made trips to the ministry in Delhi for an import licence.

The licence came through just as Data General released a newer machine with 300 MB drives that was 30 per cent cheaper. {028-S03} But the licence was for one particular model number. Murthy could take the older, costlier machine, or spend more months chasing another licence.
Ajay Shah added a connection: his book pick in an earlier episode, *The Soul of a New Machine*, was about a design project inside Data General. {#soul}

quote.text: He can’t get that because the licence is now for that particular model number.

second.caption: Narayana Murthy’s import licence

third.head: Rao’s quiet word with Sony
body: PV Narasimha Rao is often portrayed as the man who handled the politics while Manmohan Singh and Montek Singh Ahluwalia did the real work of reform. Amit Varma disagrees. Rao, he said, was a true believer. {#believer}

His evidence is a scene he wants in the series. Rao met Akio Morita, the chairman of Sony, leaned over and almost whispered that millions of Indians dreamed of nothing greater than owning a Sony television. Why not set up a factory here? {028-S09}
Morita replied, in his gentle, understated way, that he would need so many licences he would never get them.
Rao leaned in further and, in a softer voice, said: “You just apply. Leave the rest to me.” Then, Varma said, “everything that kind of happens, happens.”
third.caption: Narasimha Rao and Akio Morita

p2.title: The silent movement
p2.deck: Amit Varma’s web series in six chapters, with scenes added by Ajay Shah

sections.label: The pilot
sections.head: Marmite at St Stephen’s
sections.caption: the opening scene
body: Amit Varma’s series, *The Reformers*, has a recurring shot of a man swimming laps, explained only at the very end. The first episode proper opens on what looks like a violent clash of colours. The camera pulls back. Someone is spreading Marmite on toast.
Ajay Shah admitted that he hates Marmite. “So does the protagonist of this particular chapter,” Varma said. {028-J02}
## A room in Rudra North

The camera pulls back further. It is the early 1960s, and the room is a suite in Rudra North at St Stephen’s College, Delhi, belonging to Balbir Singh, an economics professor back from Oxford. Bade Ghulam Ali Khan is playing on the recorder, a little tinnily. Balbir Singh likes sitting with young people and talking about the world.
He wants to instil not rote learning but a spirit of debate and inquiry. That evening he talks music, not economics. At the back sits a quiet, slightly shy young Sardar: Montek Singh Ahluwalia.

Only then is the title revealed. The reforms from 1991, Varma said, had great humanitarian consequences, and the people behind them worked for higher principles with no immediate reward, much like the freedom fighters before them. {028-C01}
~ He would tell the story through five or six human stories, the ones he knew, and expected Shah to fill in some of the rest.

quote.text: A bunch of people who were fighting behind the scenes in what I think is a great freedom movement.

sections.label: Montek’s years
sections.head: Eight days in the basement
sections.caption: Montek’s years in the background
body: Montek Singh Ahluwalia’s memoir *Backstage* has a scene he barely underscores, Amit Varma said, though Indian men will know why it is moving. When he won a Rhodes Scholarship, he told his father in person. His father shook his hand, said congratulations, and that was all. {028-S02}
Ajay Shah added a detail: the young man took the train to Bombay and went to Britain by ship. A ship, Varma said, gives you time to gather your thoughts.

After Oxford and years at the World Bank, Ahluwalia answered Manmohan Singh’s call, around 1977, to come home, and worked in the background through the 1980s. Around 1990 he wrote the M document, a secret roadmap for reform, before the crisis hit.
## Locked in for India

When the reform budget had to be prepared in secrecy, 80 people, senior officers among them, were taken to the basement of the finance ministry and kept there for eight days, with dormitory beds and food brought in. {028-S05} You could check out, Varma said, borrowing from *Hotel California*, but you could never leave. {028-J05}

~ The work brought out unexpected sides of people. After the genteel, soft-spoken Ahluwalia had answered question after question from the Joint Parliamentary Committee, an MP leaving the room gave a TV reporter his verdict: “Sardarji bahut bolte hain.”

quote.text: All his father does is shake his hand and say congratulations. And that’s it, because we are just not so expressive

sections.label: The prime minister
sections.head: Too learned for Delhi
sections.caption: PV Narasimha Rao’s many lives
body: PV Narasimha Rao, Amit Varma said, was not just a politician who happened to be there in 1991. Born around 1920, he knew some ten languages, among them Telugu, Hindi, Marathi, Kannada, Urdu and Persian. When computers came to India in the 1980s, the minister taught himself to code in COBOL and BASIC. {028-S07}
Delhi never took him seriously, Varma said. Its idea of refinement was how you speak English and how you hold your cup.

Vinay Sitapati, whose *Half-Lion* Varma calls fabulous, wrote that Rao’s greatest quality was his loneliness. {028-S08} He got the top job after Rajiv Gandhi’s death partly by accident: Shankar Dayal Sharma turned it down, and Rao was seen not to be trying for it.
## A pyre and a relay

Rao died in 2004 an outcast in his own party, and the Congress did not let his body come to Delhi for a state funeral. Television showed his half-burnt pyre in Hyderabad, with stray dogs at the remains. It makes Varma angry. {028-S10}

~ Ajay Shah added a story of grace across an election. With elections coming, P Chidambaram wrote on file that inflation targeting should not be rushed through in a lame-duck administration’s last months, and left it to his successor. Arun Jaitley took it on. {028-S12}

quote.text: This was one of the greatest Indians of the twentieth century, whose actions helped lift hundreds of millions of people out of poverty.

sections.label: Two women
sections.head: Breaking through, breaking out
sections.caption: Isher Judge Ahluwalia and Padma Desai
body: Isher Judge came from a conservative Sikh family and an all-girls Marwari school in Calcutta. She went to Presidency College and then to Delhi, where for a few months she struggled with English, the language of all the economics: her school had been Hindi medium. {028-S14}

She was suspicious of slick Delhi boys with accents, but Montek Singh Ahluwalia’s sense of humour won her over, and they courted watching Godard, Truffaut and Bresson. She became, Amit Varma said, a very fine economist. He regrets leaving her memoir, *Breaking Through*, unread until after she died.
## Credit by alphabet

Padma Desai, Varma said, was a brilliant economist too often known only as Jagdish Bhagwati’s wife. {028-R04} Their 1968 book against India’s state-controlled system lists him first only by alphabetical order, yet search results credit him alone. She studied the Soviet Union for years and wrote a respected 1989 book on perestroika.
Trapped in an abusive marriage and refused a divorce, she used one of the legal grounds available, change of religion, and converted to Christianity to marry Bhagwati. {028-S15}
~ Ajay Shah recalled Bhagwati telling a dinner table that his brother, PN Bhagwati, had found the couple “living in sin” and warned that it was a crime under the IPC, “so just be careful”. {028-J11}

quote.text: The women are doubly remarkable because women are not in this game at all.

sections.label: The civil servant
sections.head: Opposition, by arrangement
sections.caption: KP Krishnan’s stories
body: KP Krishnan is the hero of the season Amit Varma would give to the 2008 financial crisis, the first India faced as part of the global economy. Varma recorded more than eight hours with him, an epic piece of oral history, he said, that Ajay Shah made possible. {028-R15}

Krishnan’s stories were also about politics. The New Pension Scheme, prepared under the Vajpayee government, was embraced by Manmohan Singh’s. Across the table sat Sushma Swaraj, now in opposition. She called it wonderful and good for the country, warned that she would have to oppose it in Parliament, and then laid out, step by step, how to get it passed. {028-S18}
## A lost decade

Then the momentum broke, by accident. After the Bombay attacks of 2008, Varma said, drawing on Puja Mehra’s *The Lost Decade*, P Chidambaram was moved to the home ministry and Pranab Mukherjee ended up at finance. He was “a complete disaster as a finance minister”, Varma said, bringing in retrospective taxation. {028-S19}
~ Krishnan, a man of deep integrity, did not hold the influential posts he should have after 2015, Varma said. Many reformers, he felt, were left out in the cold.

quote.text: Let me tell you something, in public, because I’m in the opposition, if you bring it to parliament, I will have to oppose it.
quote.who: Sushma Swaraj, as told by Amit Varma

sections.label: More anecdotes
sections.head: Opening the oil tap, slowly
sections.caption: Vijay Kelkar’s petroleum years
body: A story that means a lot to Ajay Shah is Vijay Kelkar’s journey at the petroleum ministry. When Kelkar arrived as an adviser, the state had a complete monopoly on everything petroleum: exploration, extraction, refining, distribution and petrochemicals.

Kelkar, the economist, understood the sector’s fundamental economics. Lavraj Kumar, the secretary, knew how to work the bureaucratic and political machine. Both believed there was no case for state monopolies. When Lavraj Kumar’s time ended, Kelkar, though not from the IAS, became secretary and stayed six years across governments.
Exploration, extraction, refining and petrochemicals became private. Distribution, Shah said, fumbled. {028-S23}
## Institutional memory

Such journeys take many years, Shah said, and that capability is no longer working as it used to. Ministers come and go; what carries knowledge across, he said, is a professional elite that sustains and protects its own. {028-C06}

Even the finance minister had to recruit allies one at a time. Around 1991–92, Amit Varma said, Manmohan Singh held on to Naushad Forbes’s hand after a meeting with industry leaders and whispered: “Tell the world everything you said today inside here.” {028-S24}
~ For Shah, Steven Spielberg’s *Lincoln* was an eye-opener: it skips the battles to stay with the legal fight over one amendment. “My God, it is great storytelling,” he said.

quote.text: Ministers come, ministers go, but you need this stability of the professional elite public policy in India

side.boxText: Most of Amit Varma’s scenes come from books and his long interviews: Montek Singh Ahluwalia’s *Backstage*, Vinay Sitapati’s *Half-Lion*, and more than eight hours with KP Krishnan, which Varma calls an epic piece of oral history. {028-R15}

contQuote.text: And yet, not for years, but for decades, these people don’t do what people like me do, write columns and be armchair columnists, but for years and decades these people devote their lives to playing this long game.

stories.caption: KP Krishnan’s swim
stories.kicker: Amit Varma’s recurring scene, and the man in the water
stories.head: Laps first, cabinet later
body: Every season of Amit Varma’s imagined series is punctuated by one image. From high above, a tiny glistening blue speck sits in a mass of land. The camera drops until the speck becomes a large swimming pool, and the specks in it become the arms of a man swimming from one end to the other.

The scene would return in quiet moments across nine or ten seasons. {#seasons} Someone comes to talk to the swimmer; he says something; they leave; he keeps swimming. The audience would not know what it means until the series ends, on the same shot.

The swimmer is KP Krishnan, for whom swimming is a non-negotiable part of his regimen. During a cabinet meeting that went on and on, he asked if he could step out for an hour. {#cabinet} Asked what was so urgent, he said he wanted to swim, and then come back.

Varma learnt this first-hand. His interview with Krishnan, more than eight hours long, could have been recorded in three sessions but took four. {#sessions} One of them, at a conference in Kochi, ran into his swimming time of six o’clock. Krishnan had checked out the pool earlier. “Sir, please go,” Varma told him.
He respects that, Varma said: conviction and force of will about one’s own routines, not just the larger things.
The scene, he said, is a great metaphor for the reformer’s life: you are swimming alone. {028-S01}
~ “Someone interrupts you at one point and you send him away, you continue to swim,” Varma said. “And right at the end, the last scene, you’re still swimming alone.”
stories.why: Reform is a long swim taken alone. Varma marvelled that such people gave not years but decades to a cause few understood, instead of writing columns from an armchair, as he does. {028-C07}

stories.caption: the panel that vanished
stories.kicker: How the Lehman crisis emptied a Delhi stage
stories.head: And then there were none
body: The season on the 2008 crisis, Amit Varma said, would open in a dimly lit basement in Delhi with no phone signal. On stage, Ajay Shah is moderating a panel: KP Krishnan of the finance ministry, RBI governor Subbarao and Bhave of SEBI.

A man walks up and whispers in Krishnan’s ear. Krishnan gets up and leaves. Another whispers to Subbarao, who leaves, then another to Bhave. “And you’re suddenly moderating a conversation with no participants,” Varma said. {028-S16}
Lehman Brothers had collapsed. Finance minister P Chidambaram, unable to reach any of the three on their phones, had got calls through to their drivers instead.
~ The audience, Varma added, would not have minded, “because you’re on stage and you’re so beautiful”. {028-J15}
stories.why: When a crisis breaks, the people running the system vanish from public view. How they handled 2008, Varma said, is incredibly inspiring, and deserves a season of its own, perhaps two.
stories.postscript: Shah’s own memory of the night before: hours watching the price of ICICI Bank’s ADR in New York. It barely moved. {028-C11}

stories.start: there was some important financial sector reform that Krishna really wanted
stories.end: And from this angle, from this lens, Pradam Mukraj says take a karu.
stories.caption: the postcard that won over Pranab
stories.kicker: KP Krishnan’s two-slide pitch to Pranab Mukherjee
stories.head: Two slides and a postcard
body: KP Krishnan wanted an important financial-sector reform, and Pranab Mukherjee’s instinctive socialist, 1970s self, Amit Varma said, would have revolted at it. So Krishnan brought him a presentation of two slides.
The first was a postcard to Mukherjee from a constituent in Bengal, Sharmishtha Bandopadhyay, which he had read out. Her life savings were gone, and it was up to him to do something. {028-S20}

By the end Mukherjee was furious. “Why are you reading this out for me? What do you want?” he demanded. {#furious} Krishnan said the current system ruins common people like her, and proposed the reform. Mukherjee approved it on the spot.
~ Varma loves the way Krishnan, a side player in one of the ministries in 1991, worked out how to present such reforms to politicians so they happened right away.
stories.why: Financial reform bores most audiences, Varma said, yet it shapes everyone’s life. Krishnan’s trick was to start with one named person the system had ruined. Reformers and storytellers alike, Varma said, need such ways to tell it. {028-C08}

stories.start: Okay, which I think uh NK Sing told me at some point.
stories.end: had a certain smell, then it meant that that person was from India
stories.caption: the suit that smelled of India
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on a trade ban you could smell
stories.head: Eau de licence raj
body: Ajay Shah had the story from NK Singh. In an elevator at the IMF, one man turned round without looking and said to the person behind him: “You’re from India, aren’t you?” He was right. How did he know?

The answer lay in the suit. Anyone who is, in Shah’s words, “an unfortunate owner of a thing called a suit” must have it dry-cleaned, and dry cleaning signals class, since the poor cannot afford it. {028-J07}

India had banned imports of the correct dry-cleaning fluids as luxuries. Indian dry cleaners used bad petrochemicals instead, which left a distinctive stink. {028-S06} A suit with that smell, Shah said, belonged to someone from India.
~ Later he called the story “the psychic dynamite that makes things happen”.
stories.why: Protectionism left traces on ordinary life, down to the smell of a suit. Shah counts such small humiliations, with the bruise of watching East Asia grow rich, among the forces that made India’s elite rethink. {028-C03}
stories.postscript: Varma wants one scene in the series set in a dry cleaner’s.

quiz.q: Why could Narayana Murthy not buy Data General’s newer, cheaper computer in 1983?
quiz.a: His import licence was for one particular model number, the older machine.

quiz.q: What gave away an Indian in an IMF elevator, in the story NK Singh told Ajay Shah?
quiz.a: The stink of bad petrochemicals Indian dry cleaners used after fluid imports were banned.

quiz.q: Which two computer languages did PV Narasimha Rao teach himself to code fluently in?
quiz.a: COBOL and BASIC, after computers came to India in the 1980s.

quiz.q: How did Padma Desai free herself from an abusive first marriage to marry Jagdish Bhagwati?
quiz.a: She converted to Christianity, since change of religion was a legal ground for divorce.

quiz.q: What did Arun Jaitley say when KP Krishnan urged him to think harder about inflation targeting?
quiz.a: Two of India’s finest legal and economic minds had agreed: who was he to disagree?

quiz.q: Lehman had collapsed and nobody’s phone worked in the basement. How did Chidambaram reach his officials?
quiz.a: He got calls through to their drivers, and someone whispered to each on stage.
